prompt:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle with incentre $I$. A point $P$ in the interior of the triangle satisfies
$$\angle PBA+\angle PCA = \angle PBC+\angle PCB.$$
Show that $AP \ge AI$, and that equality holds if and only if $P = I$.
answer: Proof: the condition gives $\angle BPC=90^\circ+\frac A2=\angle BIC$, so $P$ lies on the circle through $B,I,C$, whose centre is the midpoint $M$ of arc $BC$ on line $AI$; then $AP+PM\ge AM=AI+IM$ with $PM=IM$.

solutions.title: Incentre–excentre circle
solutions.body:
Write $\beta=\angle ABC$, $\gamma=\angle ACB$, $\alpha=\angle BAC$.

**$P$ lies on circle $BIC$.** Since $P$ is inside the triangle, $\angle PBA=\beta-\angle PBC$ and $\angle PCA=\gamma-\angle PCB$. The condition becomes $\beta+\gamma=2(\angle PBC+\angle PCB)$, so
$$\angle BPC=180^\circ-\frac{\beta+\gamma}{2}=90^\circ+\frac{\alpha}{2}.$$
Also $\angle BIC=180^\circ-\frac\beta2-\frac\gamma2=90^\circ+\frac\alpha2$. As $P$ and $I$ lie on the same side of $BC$ and see $BC$ under the same angle, $P$ lies on the arc $BIC$ of the circle through $B,I,C$.

**The centre of that circle.** Let the bisector $AI$ meet the circumcircle of $ABC$ again at $M$, the midpoint of arc $BC$ not containing $A$. Then $\angle MBC=\angle MAC=\frac\alpha2$, so
$$\angle MBI=\frac\alpha2+\frac\beta2,\qquad \angle MIB=\angle IAB+\angle IBA=\frac\alpha2+\frac\beta2$$
(exterior angle of triangle $ABI$). Hence $MB=MI$, and similarly $MC=MI$. So $M$ is the centre of circle $BIC$ and $MP=MI$.

**The inequality.** $A,I,M$ are collinear with $I$ between $A$ and $M$, so by the triangle inequality
$$AP+PM\ \ge\ AM=AI+IM=AI+PM,$$
i.e. $AP\ge AI$. Equality holds iff $P$ lies on segment $AM$; the only point of segment $AM$ at distance $MI$ from $M$ is $I$. So equality holds iff $P=I$ (and $P=I$ clearly satisfies the condition). ∎

prompt:
Let $P$ be a regular $2006$-gon. A diagonal of $P$ is called *good* if its endpoints divide the boundary of $P$ into two parts, each composed of an odd number of sides of $P$. The sides of $P$ are also called good.

Suppose $P$ has been dissected into triangles by $2003$ diagonals, no two of which have a common point in the interior of $P$. Find the maximum number of isosceles triangles having two good sides that could appear in such a configuration.

solutions.title: Assign two private sides to each such triangle
solutions.body:
For a chord $XY$ (side or diagonal) the two boundary arcs have $u$ and $2006-u$ sides; these have the same parity, so "good" means $u$ odd. Call an isosceles triangle with two good sides *special*.

**Construction with $1003$.** Label the vertices $V_0,\dots,V_{2005}$ and draw the $1003$ diagonals $V_0V_2, V_2V_4,\dots,V_{2004}V_0$. Each cuts off a triangle $V_{2i}V_{2i+1}V_{2i+2}$ whose two equal sides are sides of $P$ (good). Triangulate the remaining $1003$-gon with $1000$ more diagonals: $2003$ diagonals in total and $1003$ special triangles.

**Structure of a special triangle.** Let a triangle of the dissection have vertices on $P$ cutting the boundary into arcs of $u,v,w$ sides, $u+v+w=2006$. The side opposite to arc $u$ has length determined by $\min(u,2006-u)$; two sides are equal iff the corresponding arcs are equal (if $u\neq v$ but $u=2006-v$, then $w=0$). Since $u+v+w$ is even, the number of odd arcs is $0$ or $2$. In a special triangle exactly two arcs are odd and two arcs are equal; these must be the same two arcs. So a special triangle $T$ has two *legs* whose arcs (the arcs cut off by the legs, away from $T$) have the same odd length $u$, with $2u<2006$, so $u\le 1001$. Call these two arcs the *leg arcs* of $T$ and, for a leg arc $\lambda$ of $T$, let $R(\lambda)$ be the part of $P$ cut off by that leg on the side of $\lambda$ (it does not contain $T$).

**Fact 1.** If a special triangle $T'$ lies inside $R(\lambda)$, then both leg arcs of $T'$ are contained in $\lambda$. Indeed all vertices of $T'$ lie on $\lambda$, so two of its arcs lie inside $\lambda$ and the third contains the complement of $\lambda$, which has at least $2006-1001>1001$ sides, so it is not a leg arc.

**Fact 2.** If leg arcs $\lambda$ (of $T$) and $\lambda'$ (of $T'\ne T$) share a side, then one of $T,T'$ lies inside the region of the other's leg arc, i.e. $T'\subset R(\lambda)$ or $T\subset R(\lambda')$. Indeed the two legs do not cross, so the arcs are nested, disjoint, or together cover the boundary; the last is impossible ($1001+1001<2006$) and disjoint is excluded. If $\lambda=\lambda'$ the legs coincide and $T,T'$ are both the triangle adjacent to this chord on the side away from $\lambda$, so $T=T'$. If $\lambda'\subsetneq\lambda$, the leg of $T'$ is a side of $P$ on $\lambda$ or a diagonal inside $R(\lambda)$; in both cases the triangles adjacent to it on the side away from $\lambda'$ lie in $R(\lambda)$, so $T'\subset R(\lambda)$. The case $\lambda\subsetneq\lambda'$ is symmetric.

**Fact 3.** For each leg arc $\lambda$ of a special triangle $T$, some side of $P$ on $\lambda$ lies in no leg arc of a special triangle inside $R(\lambda)$. Consider the special triangles inside $R(\lambda)$ that are *maximal*, i.e. not inside the leg region of another special triangle inside $R(\lambda)$. Every special triangle inside $R(\lambda)$ lies in the leg region of a maximal one (follow a chain of nested regions upwards), so by Fact 1 its leg arcs lie in a leg arc of a maximal one. By Fact 2 the leg arcs of distinct maximal triangles are disjoint, and the two leg arcs of one triangle are disjoint. Hence the union of all leg arcs inside $\lambda$ has $\sum 2u_i$ sides — an even number. As $\lambda$ has an odd number of sides, some side of $\lambda$ is not covered.

**The bound.** For every special triangle $T$ and each of its two leg arcs $\lambda$, choose a side as in Fact 3 and *assign* it to $T$. Suppose a side $e$ were assigned to $T$ (from leg arc $\lambda$) and to $T'\ne T$ (from $\lambda'$). Then $\lambda,\lambda'$ share $e$, so by Fact 2, say, $T'\subset R(\lambda)$; but then $e$ lies in a leg arc of a special triangle inside $R(\lambda)$, contradicting the choice for $T$. (Two leg arcs of the same triangle are disjoint, so $T$ itself receives two different sides.) Thus the special triangles receive pairwise disjoint pairs of sides, and there are at most $2006/2=1003$ of them.

**Answer: 1003**

prompt:
Determine the least real number $M$ such that the inequality
$$\left|ab(a^2-b^2)+bc(b^2-c^2)+ca(c^2-a^2)\right| \le M\left(a^2+b^2+c^2\right)^2$$
holds for all real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$.

solutions.title: Factor, then AM–GM twice
solutions.body:
**Factorisation.** The polynomial $F=ab(a^2-b^2)+bc(b^2-c^2)+ca(c^2-a^2)$ vanishes when $a=b$, $b=c$ or $c=a$, so it is divisible by $(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)$; the quotient has degree $1$ and is symmetric, so it is $\lambda(a+b+c)$. Comparing at $(a,b,c)=(0,1,2)$ ($F=-6$) gives $\lambda=-1$:
$$|F|=|(a-b)(b-c)(c-a)(a+b+c)|.$$

**Upper bound.** $|F|$ and the right side are symmetric, so assume $a\le b\le c$. Put $s=a+b+c$ and $T=(a-b)^2+(b-c)^2+(c-a)^2$; note $3(a^2+b^2+c^2)=T+s^2$.
1. By AM–GM, $(b-a)(c-b)\le\left(\frac{c-a}{2}\right)^2$, so $|F|\le\frac14 (c-a)^3|s|$.
2. Since $(c-a)^2=\bigl((b-a)+(c-b)\bigr)^2\le 2\bigl((b-a)^2+(c-b)^2\bigr)$, we get $3(c-a)^2\le 2T$, i.e. $(c-a)^2\le\frac{2T}{3}$. Hence
$$|F|\le\frac14\sqrt{\left(\tfrac{2T}{3}\right)^3 s^2}=\frac{2\sqrt2}{4}\sqrt{\left(\tfrac T3\right)^3 s^2}.$$
3. By AM–GM on four numbers, $T+s^2=\frac T3+\frac T3+\frac T3+s^2\ge 4\sqrt[4]{\left(\tfrac T3\right)^3s^2}$, so $\sqrt{\left(\tfrac T3\right)^3s^2}\le\frac{(T+s^2)^2}{16}$.

Combining, $|F|\le\frac{\sqrt2}{2}\cdot\frac{(T+s^2)^2}{16}=\frac{\sqrt2}{32}\cdot 9(a^2+b^2+c^2)^2=\frac{9\sqrt2}{32}(a^2+b^2+c^2)^2$.

**Equality is attained.** We need $b-a=c-b$ and $\frac T3=s^2$. Take $a=b-1$, $c=b+1$: then $T=6$, so we need $s=3b=\sqrt2$, $b=\frac{\sqrt2}{3}$. Check: $|F|=1\cdot1\cdot2\cdot\sqrt2=2\sqrt2$ and $a^2+b^2+c^2=3b^2+2=\frac83$, so $\frac{9\sqrt2}{32}\cdot\frac{64}{9}=2\sqrt2$. Thus no smaller $M$ works.

**Answer:** $M=\dfrac{9\sqrt2}{32}$

prompt:
Determine all pairs $(x, y)$ of integers such that
$$1 + 2^x + 2^{2x+1} = y^2.$$

solutions.title: Factor $y^2-1$ and compare powers of 2
solutions.body:
All four pairs work: $1+1+2=4$ and $1+16+512=529=23^2$. If $(x,y)$ is a solution so is $(x,-y)$, so take $y\ge 0$.

**$x<0$ is impossible.** For $x=-1$ the left side is $1+\frac12+\frac12=2$, not a square. For $x\le-2$, $0<2^x+2^{2x+1}<1$, so the left side is not an integer.

**$x=0$** gives $y^2=4$, $y=2$. **$x=1,2$** give $11$ and $37$, not squares. So let $x\ge3$.

**Setting up.** Write the equation as $2^x(1+2^{x+1})=(y-1)(y+1)$. The left side is even, so $y$ is odd, and $y-1,y+1$ are consecutive even numbers: one of them is $\equiv2\pmod 4$. Since $1+2^{x+1}$ is odd, the product $(y-1)(y+1)$ contains exactly $x$ factors $2$, so the other factor contains exactly $x-1$ factors $2$. Hence
$$y=2^{x-1}m+\varepsilon,\qquad m\ \text{odd},\ \varepsilon=\pm1,$$
and $m>0$ because $y>0$. Substituting, $y^2-1=2^{2x-2}m^2+2^x m\varepsilon=2^x+2^{2x+1}$; dividing by $2^x$:
$$2^{x-2}m^2+m\varepsilon=1+2^{x+1}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 1-\varepsilon m=2^{x-2}(m^2-8).$$

**$\varepsilon=1$:** $1-m\le 0$, so $m^2\le 8$, $m=1$; then $0=-7\cdot 2^{x-2}$, false.

**$\varepsilon=-1$:** $1+m=2^{x-2}(m^2-8)>0$, so $m\ge3$; since $x\ge 3$, $1+m\ge 2(m^2-8)$, i.e. $2m^2-m-17\le0$, which forces $m\le3$. So $m=3$: $4=2^{x-2}$, $x=4$, and $y=2^3\cdot3-1=23$.

**Answer:** $(0,2),(0,-2),(4,23),(4,-23)$.

prompt:
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial of degree $n>1$ with integer coefficients and let $k$ be a positive integer. Consider the polynomial
$$Q(x) = P(P(\ldots P(P(x))\ldots)),$$
where $P$ occurs $k$ times. Prove that there are at most $n$ integers $t$ such that $Q(t) = t$.
answer: Proof: using $a-b\mid P(a)-P(b)$, every integer periodic point of $P$ has period $1$ or $2$; if a $2$-cycle $u\leftrightarrow v$ exists, every integer $t$ with $P(P(t))=t$ satisfies $t+P(t)=u+v$, a degree-$n$ equation.

solutions.title: Periodic points have period at most 2
solutions.body:
We use repeatedly: for integers $a,b$, $a-b\mid P(a)-P(b)$ (since $a-b\mid a^j-b^j$).

**Claim 1. If $Q(t)=t$ for an integer $t$, then $P(P(t))=t$.** Let $x_0=t$, $x_{i+1}=P(x_i)$, so $x_k=x_0$ and the sequence is periodic. By the divisibility,
$$x_0-x_1\mid x_1-x_2\mid x_2-x_3\mid\cdots\mid x_k-x_{k+1}=x_0-x_1,$$
so all differences $x_i-x_{i+1}$ have the same absolute value $d$. If $d=0$, $P(t)=t$. If $d>0$, the differences $x_{i+1}-x_i$ ($0\le i<k$) sum to $x_k-x_0=0$, so they are not all equal; hence for some $i$, $x_{i+2}-x_{i+1}=-(x_{i+1}-x_i)$, i.e. $x_{i+2}=x_i$. Then the $P$-orbit of $x_i$ is $\{x_i,x_{i+1}\}$; as the whole sequence is periodic, $t$ belongs to this orbit, so $P(P(t))=t$. $\square$

**Case A: every such $t$ satisfies $P(t)=t$.** Then the $t$'s are roots of $P(x)-x$, a polynomial of degree $n\ge 2$, so there are at most $n$ of them.

**Case B: there are integers $u\ne v$ with $P(u)=v$, $P(v)=u$.**

**Claim 2.** Every integer $t$ with $P(P(t))=t$ satisfies $t+P(t)=u+v$.

Let $t'=P(t)$. If $\{t,t'\}=\{u,v\}$ this is clear. Otherwise $t\notin\{u,v\}$ and $t'\notin\{u,v\}$ (if, say, $t'=u$ then $t=P(t')=v$). Then
$$u-t\mid P(u)-P(t)=v-t'\mid P(v)-P(t')=u-t,$$
so $|u-t|=|v-t'|\ne0$; similarly $|u-t'|=|v-t|\ne0$.
- If $u-t=v-t'$ and $u-t'=v-t$, subtracting gives $t'-t=t-t'$, so $t=t'$, and then $u=v$ — contradiction.
- Otherwise $u-t=-(v-t')$ or $u-t'=-(v-t)$; either way $u+v=t+t'$. $\square$

So all integers $t$ with $Q(t)=t$ (which satisfy $P(P(t))=t$ by Claim 1) are roots of $P(x)+x-(u+v)$, a polynomial of degree $n$ (as $n>1$). There are at most $n$ of them. ∎

prompt:
Assign to each side $b$ of a convex polygon $P$ the maximum area of a triangle that has $b$ as a side and is contained in $P$.

Show that the sum of the areas assigned to the sides of $P$ is at least twice the area of $P$.
answer: Proof: lemma — every convex $2n$-gon (angles of $180^\circ$ allowed) of area $S$ has a side and a vertex spanning a triangle of area $\ge S/n$ (the triangles cut out by consecutive main diagonals cover the polygon); then subdivide each side $a_i$ into $k_i$ pieces with $\sum k_i=2n$ and $k_i/n$ slightly above $S_i/S$ to get a contradiction.

solutions.title: Main diagonals of a subdivided polygon (official solution, reworded)
solutions.body:
Allow "convex polygons" to have angles equal to $180^\circ$ (extra vertices on sides). Write $[\cdot]$ for area.

**Lemma.** Let $V_0V_1\dots V_{2n-1}$ ($n\ge2$) be such a convex $2n$-gon of area $S$ in which no $n+1$ consecutive vertices are collinear. Then some side $V_jV_{j+1}$ and some vertex span a triangle of area $\ge S/n$.

*Proof.* Indices are mod $2n$, the polygon is labelled counterclockwise. The *main diagonals* $V_jV_{j+n}$ pass through the interior (no $n+1$ consecutive vertices are collinear). Let $\ell_j$ be the directed line $V_j\to V_{j+n}$; then $\ell_{j+n}$ is $\ell_j$ reversed. The diagonals $V_jV_{j+n}$ and $V_{j+1}V_{j+n+1}$ have alternating endpoints, so they cross at an interior point $P_j$ (and $P_{j+n}=P_j$). Let $\Delta_j$ be the triangle $V_jV_{j+1}P_j$.

*The $\Delta_j$ cover the polygon.* Take a point $X$ of the polygon on no main diagonal. Since $X$ is on opposite sides of $\ell_0$ and $\ell_n$, the cyclic sequence "is $X$ left of $\ell_j$?" ($j=0,\dots,2n-1$) is not constant, so for some $j$, $X$ is left of $\ell_j$ and right of $\ell_{j+1}$. The vertices strictly left of $\ell_j$ are $V_{j+1},\dots,V_{j+n-1}$ and those strictly right of $\ell_{j+1}$ are $V_{j+n+2},\dots,V_j$; so the angular region at $P_j$ left of $\ell_j$ and right of $\ell_{j+1}$ is the one bounded by the rays $P_jV_j$ and $P_jV_{j+1}$, and its intersection with the polygon is exactly $\Delta_j$ (the boundary between $V_j$ and $V_{j+1}$ is a single side). So $X\in\Delta_j$. Points on main diagonals form a set of zero area, hence $\sum_{j=0}^{2n-1}[\Delta_j]\ge S$.

*Picking a good pair.* Group the $2n$ triangles into $n$ pairs $\{\Delta_j,\Delta_{j+n}\}$; some pair has $[\Delta_j]+[\Delta_{j+n}]\ge S/n$. Write $A=V_j$, $B=V_{j+1}$, $A'=V_{j+n}$, $B'=V_{j+n+1}$, $P=P_j=AA'\cap BB'$, and by symmetry assume $PB\ge PB'$. Triangles $PBA'$ and $PB'A'$ have bases $PB$, $PB'$ on the same line and the same apex $A'$, so $[PBA']\ge[PB'A']$. As $P$ lies on segment $AA'$,
$$[ABA']=[ABP]+[PBA']\ge[ABP]+[PA'B']=[\Delta_j]+[\Delta_{j+n}]\ge\frac Sn,$$
and $ABA'$ is spanned by the side $AB$ and the vertex $A'$. $\square$

**Main proof.** Let $P$ have area $S$ and sides $a_1,\dots,a_m$, and let $S_i$ be the number assigned to $a_i$. If $m=3$, each $S_i=S$ and the sum is $3S$. Let $m\ge4$; then $S_i<S$ (a triangle with area $S$ inside $P$ would be all of $P$). Suppose, for contradiction, $\sum S_i/S<2$.

Since $\sum S_i/S<2\le m$, we can choose reals $r_i$ with $S_i/S<r_i<1$ and $\sum r_i=2$ (e.g. $r_i=S_i/S+\theta(1-S_i/S)$ for a suitable $\theta\in(0,1)$), and then rationals $q_i$ so close to $r_i$ that still $S_i/S<q_i<1$ and $\sum q_i=2$. Write $q_i=k_i/n$ with a common denominator $n$; then $k_i$ are positive integers, $k_i<n$, and $\sum k_i=2n$.

Divide each side $a_i$ into $k_i$ equal pieces. This gives a convex $2n$-gon of area $S$, and since every $k_i<n$, no $n+1$ consecutive vertices are collinear. By the lemma there is a piece $b$ of some side $a_i$ and a vertex $H$ with $[bH]\ge S/n$. The triangle with base $a_i$ and apex $H$ has the same height and a base $k_i$ times longer, and it lies in $P$ by convexity, so
$$S_i\ \ge\ k_i\cdot\frac Sn=q_iS>S_i,$$
a contradiction. Hence $\sum S_i\ge 2S$. ∎
